How PubPeer Comments works

This module checks references and warns for citations that have comments on pubpeer (excluding Statcheck comments).

The PubPeer module uses the PubPeer API to check for each reference that has a DOI whether there are comments on the post-publication peer review platform. If comments are found, a link to the comments is provided. Comments by ‘Statcheck’ on PubPeer are ignored, see https://retractionwatch.com/2016/09/02/heres-why-more-than-50000-psychology-studies-are-about-to-have-pubpeer-entries/.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

For more information, see PubPeer.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How RetractionWatch works

This module checks references and warns for citations in the RetractionWatch Database.

The RetractionWatch Check module compares the reference list against studies in the RetractionWatch database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that the study was retracted, has an expression of concern, or a correction.

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the authors are already aware that a study was retracted, but the module can’t evaluate this.

The database can be manually updated with the rw_update function. For more information, see https://gitlab.com/crossref/retraction-watch-data.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens and Lisa DeBruine

Read more in the metacheck manual.

How Replication Check works

This module checks references and warns for citations of original studies for which replication or reproduction studies exist in the FLoRA database.

The Replication Check module compares the reference list against studies in the FLoRA (FORRT Library of Replication Attempts) database based on the DOI. If a study in the database is found, a reminder is provided that a replication or reproduction of the original study exists, and should be cited. No reminder is given when the paper already cites that replication or reproduction (matched by its DOI).

The module requires that the reference has a DOI: the DOI in the paper’s reference list, or one looked up with add_bib_match() before the module runs (see ref_table()). References without a DOI are not checked.

It is possible the original study was cited for other reasons than the empirical claim tested, or that the replication/reproduction in the FLoRA database is for only one of the studies in the paper, and not the study the authors discuss.

The database can be manually updated with the FLoRA_update() function. For more information, see https://forrt.org/FLoRA/.

This module was developed by Daniel Lakens, Lisa DeBruine and Lukas Wallrich

Read more in the metacheck manual.

Full text

Abstract

Watching someone in danger can make a viewer feel anxious even when they know they are safe.

Studying how this response builds, persists and subsides requires methods that capture experience as events unfold. We present an open-source browser platform for continuous affect rating and demonstrate its use with a 13.5-minute film of unsecured skyscraper climbing. Viewers rate valence and arousal simultaneously on an affect grid embedded in the video. The platform records ratings alongside video and displayed-frame timestamps, pauses playback during interruptions, and combines participant training with input logging and checks on session quality. An exploratory sample (𝑛 = 21) informed preregistered tests in an independent confirmatory sample (𝑁 = 124). Arousal rose as the climb progressed, remained elevated for several minutes, and then declined, with the sustained period experienced as most unpleasant. Group-level time courses closely reproduced across samples (arousal 𝑟 = .993; valence 𝑟 = .937). Self-reported somatic anxiety increased substantially after viewing (𝑑 𝑧 = 1.03), and larger increases were associated with higher arousal and more unpleasant valence during the film. The platform, analysis code and reference data are openly available. Together, these resources support online characterisation of naturalistic stimuli and provide a shared temporal reference for studying sustained emotion, bodily experience and their physiological and neural correlates.

Moment-to-Moment Affect During Film-Induced Somatic Anxiety

Watching someone hang from the edge of a skyscraper can be uncomfortable even from the safety of a chair. As the danger unfolds, concern for the person on screen may be accompanied by tension and other bodily sensations. Such films offer a way to study emotion as it builds, persists and subsides. Capturing these changes requires measurements made during the episode rather than only afterwards (Saarimäki, 2021). Here we present an open-source browser platform for continuous affect rating and use it to characterise a film of sustained vicarious danger, examining both the reproducibility of its affective time course and changes in viewers' reported bodily anxiety.

Films are widely used for emotion induction because they present the same unfolding events to every viewer. Established film libraries have typically been characterised using ratings collected after viewing (Gilman et al., 2017; Gross & Levenson, 1995; Schaefer et al., 2010).

These ratings describe the overall experience but do not show when emotion intensifies, remains elevated or begins to recede. Continuous ratings trace experience within the film (Ruef & Levenson, 2007), and have been related to neural responses and brain-state dynamics during naturalistic viewing (Chang et al., 2021; Goldin et al., 2005). The Emo-FilM dataset combines moment-to-moment emotion annotations with physiological and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) recordings (Morgenroth et al., 2025), while continuous anxiety ratings have been used to follow the suspense of a Hitchcock thriller (Kirk & Robinson, 2024). Such approaches allow researchers to examine emotional episodes through their changing course.

Online testing makes it possible to collect these ratings from many viewers, but introduces challenges for interpreting them. A rating must be linked to the images actually presented, and researchers need to know whether viewing and responding proceeded as intended. Buffering or switching to another browser tab can disrupt stimulus exposure, while periods without input may reflect either stable feelings or disengagement. Unsupervised studies must also contend with AI-assisted and automated responding, which complicate the assessment of participation (Sehgal et al., 2026; Veselovsky et al., 2023; Westwood, 2025). Recording the circumstances in which ratings were made is therefore part of establishing what those ratings can tell us.

Existing tools support continuous annotation in browsers (Boccignone et al., 2017; Farrens et al., 2020; Louven et al., 2022; Melhart et al., 2019), on desktop computers (Girard, 2014; Girard & Wright, 2018), and in immersive virtual reality (Fourcade et al., 2025). Our platform brings simultaneous affect rating, controlled presentation and records of participation together in one open workflow. Viewers move a point within an affect grid embedded in the video to report how pleasant and activating their experience feels, building on established dimensional and continuous rating methods (Russell, 1980; Russell et al., 1989; Schubert, 1999). Each rating is stored with the video time and, where supported by the browser, the time of the displayed frame. Viewing interruptions pause the film and are logged, while periodic saving allows sessions to resume after a page reload. Participants practise before viewing, and input and text-entry records support subsequent checks on session quality (Online Resource 1, Fig. S1).

We demonstrate the platform with a 13.5-min first-person film of people climbing and performing unsecured stunts on a skyscraper. Presented without sound, the film conveys danger without requiring dialogue and builds towards a prolonged period of exposure at height (Figure 1a). This makes it a candidate stimulus for studying sustained unpleasant arousal and the transitions into and out of that state. To assess whether the experience also changes reported bodily anxiety, participants completed the somatic subscale of the State-Trait Inventory for Cognitive and Somatic Anxiety (STICSA) before and after viewing. This scale measures symptoms such as a fast heartbeat and tense muscles (Grös et al., 2007; Ree et al., 2008). Relating these reported bodily changes to the unfolding affective response connects the study of emotion dynamics with questions about interoceptive experience (Critchley & Garfinkel, 2017; Del Popolo Cristaldi et al., 2026).

An exploratory sample (𝑛 = 21) informed preregistered hypotheses tested in an independent confirmatory sample (𝑁 = 124). We predicted that arousal would rise, remain elevated and then decline; that the sustained period would be experienced as more unpleasant than the opening; and that somatic anxiety would increase after viewing. We also tested whether the group-level affective time course reproduced across samples. Further hypotheses examined whether everyday fear of heights was associated with a stronger response, whether increases in somatic anxiety accompanied higher arousal and more unpleasant valence, and whether retrospective anxiety ratings agreed with plateau arousal and somatic change.

Method Preregistration and Transparency

The hypotheses and analysis plan were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; https://osf.io/s2yvb). All confirmatory tests followed the registered plan, and exploratory analyses are labelled as such.

Rating Platform and Data Integrity

The platform is a jsPsych task (de Leeuw et al., 2023) hosted on a JATOS server (Lange et al., 2015) and runs in an ordinary desktop web browser. It is open source (MIT licence), and the version used here is archived as v1.0-heights-film (see Data Availability). Participants rate on a small affect grid (Russell et al., 1989) overlaid on the video (Figure 1a; Online Resource 1, Fig. S2). The mouse pointer is hidden and locked, so moving the mouse moves the dot without clicking. Horizontal position codes valence (0 = unpleasant,100 = pleasant) and vertical position arousal (0 = low,100 = high). The dot position is sampled at 20 Hz together with the video, frame and elapsed time, and every raw input event is stored. The film is downloaded in full before playback, playback controls and seeking are disabled, leaving the tab or full screen pauses the film, and data are saved every 30 s so that a session resumes after a page reload. Before the film, participants practise the mouse control by tracking a moving target and by placing six everyday situations on the grid, with feedback. The same session can present Likert-type scales, multiple-choice and checklist items and free-text entry. Several features support data integrity: two instructed-response attention checks, blocked pasting and logged keystrokes in text fields, counts of script-generated browser events, and quality-control code that summarises coverage, interruptions and rating activity and flags unusual mouse movement and text entry for review.

Participants were excluded by the registered rules alone (Online Resource 1, Table S1). Section S1 of Online Resource 1 describes each feature.

Participants

Participants were recruited on Prolific (Palan & Schitter, 2018). Filters required fluent English, normal or corrected-to-normal vision, an approval rate of at least 95%, at least 20 previous submissions and a desktop computer with a mouse or trackpad. Recruitment ran in cohorts with a 50/50 quota on Prolific's sex screener, and participants were paid £4.80. The information sheet advised people with a strong fear of heights not to take part. The pilot and the first cohort formed the exploratory sample, which was used to fix the segment edges, the exclusion rules and the sample size. Later cohorts formed the confirmatory sample, on which all confirmatory tests were run. Recruitment stopped at the end of the first cohort that brought the number of usable confirmatory participants to at least 120, which gives 80% power to detect correlations of about .25. The study involved watching a film and answering questionnaires and

Stimulus

The stimulus was a 13 min 28 s first-person video of an unsecured climb to the roof of a skyscraper (Tikhomirov, 2017), presented without sound (1,280 × 720 pixels, 25 frames per second).

Procedure and Measures

After consent and a device check, participants rated their everyday fear of heights ('In everyday life, how afraid are you of heights?', 1-7) and completed the practice. They then completed the somatic subscale of the STICSA with state instructions (11 items, 1-4, total 11-44; Ree et al., 2008), watched the film while rating continuously, and completed the STICSA again immediately afterwards. Instructions asked participants how they felt at that moment. Participants then rated how tense or anxious they had felt overall while watching (1-7) and answered further questions about their experience and about data quality. They also wrote an account of what they saw and how the film made them feel (at least 100 words), with a separate optional field for feedback on the study or technical difficulties.

Data Processing and Exclusions

Ratings were resampled to 1 Hz of film time (808 values) by linear interpolation. The film was divided into four preregistered segments, estimated in the exploratory sample by piecewise-linear segmentation of group-mean arousal: baseline (0-262 s), rise (262-470 s), plateau (470-692 s) and return (692-808 s). Participants were excluded if they failed both attention checks, produced script-generated input, did not type their written account (fewer than 0.2 keystrokes per character for accounts of at least 200 characters), gave erratic input (more than 10% of mouse movements larger than 250 pixels), had disrupted viewing (more than 30 s of buffering or 60 s of interruptions), rated during less than 95% of the film, or had seen the film before (Online Resource 1, Table S1).

Statistical Analysis

All tests were two-sided (𝛼 = .05) with Holm correction within each hypothesis family, and a directional hypothesis counted as supported only if the test was significant in the predicted direction. H1 compared STICSA totals after and before the film (paired 𝑡 test; 𝑑 𝑧 with exact 95% CI; Wilcoxon signed-rank test as a check). H2 tested four contrasts between participants' segment means with paired 𝑡 tests (arousal: rise > baseline, plateau > baseline, return < plateau; valence: plateau < baseline). H3 correlated the confirmatory and exploratory group-mean series (Pearson 𝑟; 95% CI from 5,000 circular block bootstrap resamples with 30-s blocks) and was supported if the lower bound exceeded .50. H4-H6 were Spearman correlations with bootstrap 95% CIs (5,000 resamples): everyday fear of heights with plateau arousal, plateau valence and STICSA change (H4); STICSA change with whole-film arousal and valence (H5); and post-film anxiety with STICSA change and plateau arousal (H6). All tests were repeated in two registered sensitivity samples (stricter engagement criteria; participants rejected on Prolific removed).

Exploratory analyses examined the change in each STICSA item (Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, Holm-corrected across items) and the effects of age and sex (mixed models of segment means).

Analyses were run in Python 3.13.7 with NumPy, SciPy, pandas and statsmodels. Large language model tools (ChatGPT and Codex, OpenAI; Claude Code, Anthropic) assisted with writing and testing the analysis code and with preparing the manuscript. The analysis code was checked with tests on small simulated datasets with known answers, and the author verified the analyses, results and references and takes full responsibility for the work.

Results

Online Implementation and Data Quality

Of 130 completed confirmatory sessions, 124 (95.4%) met the registered criteria. The exclusions were for disrupted viewing (3 sessions), an untyped written account (2) and erratic input (1); no session was excluded for script-generated input, low coverage, failing both attention checks or having seen the film. In the exploratory sample, 21 of 23 completed sessions were usable. Buffering occurred in 3 confirmatory sessions and interruptions in 7 (longest 1,795 s and 389 s), and ratings covered a median of 100% of film seconds (minimum 98.5%). Of the completed sessions, 125 passed both attention checks and 5 failed one, and 123 participants reported watching with full attention, 4 mostly and 3 not. Among retained participants, ratings changed in a median of 3.5 bouts per minute (interquartile range 1.9-5.1), and the median longest stretch without input was 77 s, which may reflect holding the dot still while feelings were unchanged. The 24 participants who met the registered definition of sparse rating were removed in the stricter sensitivity sample. Split-half reliability of the group-mean series was .992 for arousal and .979 for valence. Page reloads were not recorded in the exported data. The retained sample had a mean age of 34.2 years (𝑆𝐷 = 12.0; 59 female, 62 male, 3 not available). Sample characteristics, descriptive statistics and all confirmatory tests, including both sensitivity samples, are given in Online Resource 1 (Tables S2-S5).

Somatic Anxiety and Affective Time Course

Somatic anxiety (H1). STICSA somatic scores rose by 6.79 points, from 𝑀 = 13.76 (𝑆𝐷 = 3.56) before the film to 𝑀 = 20.55 (𝑆𝐷 = 7.29) after it, 𝑡(123) = 11.46, 𝑝 < .001, 𝑑 𝑧 = 1.03, 95% CI [0.81, 1.25] (Figure 2a). Scores rose for 109 participants and fell for 8, and the Wilcoxon test agreed (𝑇 = 197, 𝑝 < .001). In the exploratory item analysis, all eleven items increased (𝑝 Holm < .001; Figure 2b; Online Resource 1, Table S6). The largest change was in a fast heartbeat (𝑑 𝑧 = 1.17) and the smallest in a dry throat, weak muscles and stiff limbs (𝑑 𝑧 = 0.52-0.54).

Time course (H2, H3). Arousal was higher than at baseline in both the rise segment, 𝑡(123) = 14.67, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 𝑧 = 1.32, 95% CI [1.07, 1.56], and the plateau, 𝑡(123) = 19.77, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 𝑧 = 1.78, 95% CI [1.49, 2.06], and it was lower in the return segment than on the plateau, 𝑡(123) = -14.70, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 𝑧 = -1.32, 95% CI [-1.56, -1.08] (Figure 1b; Online Resource 1, Fig. S3). Valence was lower on the plateau than at baseline, 𝑡(123) = -9.85, 𝑝 Holm < .001, 𝑑 𝑧 = -0.88, 95% CI [-1.09, -0.68] (Figure 1c). The confirmatory group-mean series closely followed the shape of the exploratory series, for arousal 𝑟 = .993, 95% CI [.990, .996] and for valence 𝑟 = .937, 95% CI [.893, .966].

Individual differences (H4-H6).

Participants whose STICSA scores rose more gave higher whole-film arousal ratings, 𝜌 = .24, 95% CI [.05, .41], 𝑝 = .008, 𝑝 Holm = .008, and lower whole-film valence ratings, 𝜌 = -.38, 95% CI [-.51, -.23], 𝑝 < .001, 𝑝 Holm < .001 (Figure 2c, d).

Post-film anxiety correlated with STICSA change, 𝜌 = .56, 95% CI [.44, .67], 𝑝 < .001, 𝑝 Holm < .001, and with plateau arousal, 𝜌 = .34, 95% CI [.15, .50], 𝑝 < .001, 𝑝 Holm < .001. Everyday fear of heights was associated with more negative plateau valence, 𝜌 = -.32, 95% CI [-.46, -.16], 𝑝 < .001, 𝑝 Holm = .001. Its registered associations with plateau arousal, 𝜌 = .08, 95% CI [-.09, .26], 𝑝 = .355, 𝑝 Holm = .355, and with STICSA change, 𝜌 = .18, 95% CI [.00, .35], 𝑝 = .049, 𝑝 Holm = .098, were not supported (all individual-difference tests: Online Resource 1, Fig. S4).

Somatic anxiety and ratings by segment (exploratory).

In a post hoc exploratory analysis of both samples (𝑛 = 145), STICSA change was correlated with the mean ratings in each segment (Spearman 𝜌 with bootstrap 95% confidence intervals, uncorrected; Figure 3). At baseline there was no clear association (arousal 𝜌 = .09, 95% CI [-.07, .25], 𝑝 = .279; valence 𝜌 = -.06, 95% CI [-.22, .09], 𝑝 = .449). Valence was associated with STICSA change in the rise (𝜌 = -.38, 95% CI [-.50, -.24], 𝑝 < .001) and plateau (𝜌 = -.36, 95% CI [-.49, -.21], 𝑝 < .001), and arousal in the plateau (𝜌 = .26, 95% CI [.11, .41], 𝑝 = .001) but less clearly in the rise (𝜌 = .14, 95% CI [-.03, .31], 𝑝 = .083). In the return segment the associations were weaker (arousal 𝜌 = .19, 95% CI [.02, .34], 𝑝 = .024; valence 𝜌 = -.20, 95% CI [-.35, -.04], 𝑝 = .016).

Sensitivity and additional analyses.

All registered support decisions were unchanged in both sensitivity samples (𝑛 = 96 and 120; Online Resource 1, Table S5). In the registered descriptive analysis, segment edges re-estimated in the confirmatory sample fell at 262, 467 and 660 s, against the registered 262, 470 and 692 s. Exploratory analyses described where on the affect grid the ratings fell in each segment (Online Resource 1, Fig. S5) and found no evidence that the time course differed by sex (arousal: 𝜒 2 (3) = 0.28, 𝑝 = .964; valence: 𝜒 2 (3) = 0.72, 𝑝 = .869) or by age, or that STICSA change was associated with sex or age (Online Resource 1, Table S7 and Figs. S6-S7).

Discussion

A film of other people in danger elicited sustained unpleasant arousal in viewers who were themselves safe. The affective response followed a closely reproducible course across independent samples, and viewers reported substantially more bodily symptoms of anxiety after watching.

These findings support the film as a strong and consistent emotion-induction stimulus. The accompanying open platform provides a means of characterising how affect unfolds during naturalistic stimulation. The film's effectiveness is supported by convergence between continuous affect ratings, retrospective anxiety and reported bodily symptoms. Somatic anxiety increased in nearly nine out of ten viewers, and all confirmatory conclusions were unchanged under stricter screening.

Established film-validation studies have characterised stimuli according to the intensity and nature of the emotions they evoke (Gross & Levenson, 1995; Schaefer et al., 2010). The present findings complement this approach by characterising the progression and duration of the response, providing a sustained induction relevant to research using suspenseful films to study anxiety and brain-body interactions (Kirk & Robinson, 2024).

The film was selected specifically for naturalistic neuroimaging because it contains an extended, relatively uneventful opening, rising tension, sustained danger and a quiet ending as the climbers leave the skyscraper. Continuous ratings closely followed this intended progression. This temporal structure offers a useful basis for studying dynamic functional connectivity, including comparisons across phases and changes within periods of sustained arousal. The reproducible group trajectories also provide a reference for independently collected neural and physiological recordings. Emo-FilM demonstrates the value of this approach by combining continuous emotion annotations with physiological and fMRI data from a separate sample (Morgenroth et al., 2025).

Such reference curves can guide analyses while allowing for differences in individual experience.

The film also has practical advantages for neuroimaging. Its narrative is readily understood without sound, allowing use in scanning protocols where audio delivery is constrained. Its visually engaging events and multiple people on screen accord with calls to select naturalistic stimuli according to their content, presentation and experimental purpose (Grall & Finn, 2022). Social content may be particularly useful: Finn and Bandettini (2021) found that clips with greater social content supported stronger prediction of cognitive traits from functional connectivity. The first-person viewpoint may further promote immersion by presenting the height and movement from the climber's perspective.

Larger increases in somatic anxiety accompanied higher arousal and more unpleasant valence, with exploratory associations most evident during the rise and plateau. This links the film's affective progression to reported bodily experience and provides a setting for studying how bodily sensations are interpreted within changing emotional contexts (Del Popolo Cristaldi et al., 2026). Given the modest correspondence between subjective experience and physiology reported in previous film studies (Mauss et al., 2005), combining the task with physiological recordings could examine how felt and measured bodily responses relate during rising, sustained and declining arousal.

The platform supports this work within a browser-based workflow. Tools such as DARMA and PAGAN have already made continuous annotation more accessible (Girard & Wright, 2018; Melhart et al., 2019). The present platform combines simultaneous valence and arousal ratings within the video with participant training, video and displayed-frame timestamps, interruption handling and input records. These features allow films to be characterised online before laboratory use and support explicit quality-control decisions. Input logs also permit review of potentially assisted or automated responding, although their detection accuracy has not been established. The task, quality-control code and deployment scripts are openly available for adaptation to other stimuli.

Several questions remain for subsequent validation. Comparisons with other films could clarify the contribution of height-related danger to the observed response. Continuous rating preserved subjective emotional engagement during amusing and sad films but altered activity in regions associated with introspection (Hutcherson et al., 2005), so transfer to passive viewing warrants testing. Somatic symptoms were assessed only before and after the film, leaving their time course unresolved. Online recruitment and advice that people with a strong fear of heights should not participate also limit generalisation to those with severe height-related fear.

The platform and reference data provide a reusable basis for studying sustained emotion. Assessing session quality.

Two instructed-response attention checks are given, one before and one after the film. In text fields, pasting, dropping and copying text are blocked, and keystrokes and input types are logged. Browser events not generated by a person (script-generated input) are counted. Quality-control code computes measures of rating coverage, interruptions, buffering and rating activity, and flags a session for review if any of the following occurs: • Viewing: more than 3 interruptions or more than 60 s interrupted; more than 30 s of buffering; more than 120 s away from the window; more than 180 s of film without any rating input.

• Training: tracking error above 20 units after the last run; fewer than 3 of the 6 situations placed correctly.

• Mouse movement: 3 or more isolated large jumps (a single movement of more than 250 pixels with no other mouse event within 100 ms on either side); more than 10% of movements larger than 250 pixels; 30 or more identical consecutive movements of at least 3 pixels; 98% or more of movements along one axis only (with at least 200 movements).

• Text entry: fewer than 0.2 keystrokes per character (texts of at least 200 characters); typing faster than 700 characters per minute; two or more different phrasing markers (below); 80% or more similarity to another participant's text (sequence-matching ratio).

The phrasing markers are words and characters that are common in text produced by large language models and rare in quick participant writing: delve, tapestry, navigate/navigating the, testament to, in conclusion, overall,, it's worth noting, as an AI, language model, visceral, palpable, juxtapose (and related forms), underscore(s/d), a sense of awe/unease/vertigo, heightened sense, multifaceted and the em dash. A match is a reason to read the text, not evidence of assistance: several markers are words an attentive viewer of this film could use. Flags only prompted review; participants were excluded solely by the registered rules (Table S1), which overlap with some of these criteria. The written account served as evidence about participation; analysis of its content is outside the scope of this report.

S1. The Rating Platform

This section describes the platform (version v1.0-heights-film) in more detail than the main text. Code references are to the archived release; the platform documentation gives the full event definitions. Figure S1 shows the session workflow.

Recording ratings.

A small affect grid is overlaid on the lower right of the video (Figure S2). The mouse pointer is hidden and locked, so moving the mouse moves the dot without clicking; arrow keys provide an alternative. Horizontal position codes valence (0 = unpleasant,100 = pleasant) and vertical position arousal (0 = low,100 = high). The position is sampled at 20 Hz, and each sample stores the video time, the media time of the last frame presented (where the browser reports it), the elapsed time since the film started and whether the film was playing. Every input event is also stored unsmoothed, so that the rating series can be reconstructed from the raw input.

Controlling presentation.

The whole film is downloaded before playback starts, and sessions that cannot download it within 5 min end early. Player controls are hidden and seeking is blocked. Hiding the tab, leaving full screen or losing the pointer lock pauses the film behind a 'Continue' screen, and the number and duration of such interruptions, as well as any buffering, are logged. Data are sent to the server every 30 s of film; after a page reload, the session resumes shortly before the last saved point.

Training.

Before the film, participants practise with the same pointer-locked mouse control in two steps.

First, for 40 s they keep the dot on an orange target that moves around the grid without the film: it rests for 6 s in each corner and 4 s at the centre, then glides diagonally to a final point, so that every combination of valence and arousal is visited. Accuracy is the mean distance between dot and target (0-100 units), ignoring the first 1.5 s after each jump of the target; if it exceeds 20 units, the practice is repeated once.

Second, a page explains the grid: left to right is unpleasant to pleasant, with neutral in the centre; down to up is low to high activation, where activation means 'feeling activated or stirred up, regardless of whether the feeling is pleasant or unpleasant'. It adds that the same area can hold quite different feelings: being nervous and being angry are both unpleasant with high activation (upper left), while being sad or bored is unpleasant with low activation (lower left). Participants then read six situations in random order. For each, they move the dot to where that feeling belongs and press the space bar; the expected quadrant is then highlighted and a one-sentence explanation is shown. A placement counts as correct if it lies in the expected quadrant at least 5 units from both midlines. The six situations, with the expected quadrant and the explanation shown, were: 1.

'You are waiting for important test results and your heart is pounding.' Unpleasant, high activation: 'Feeling nervous or tense is unpleasant, with high activation.' 2. 'Someone pushes in front of you in a long queue and you feel your face getting hot.' Unpleasant, high activation: 'Anger is also unpleasant with high activation -this area holds many different feelings, not just fear.'
